¶
'''unpliantly''' (un-plī′ant-li), ''adv.'' In an unpliant manner; uncompliäntly.

'''unplight<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''unpliȝt''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> (intensive) + ''plight''<sup>1</sup>.] Peril.

'''unplight<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''unplighten'', prop. ''unpliten'', var. of ''unpleiten'', mod. E. ''unplait'', as ''plight''<sup>3</sup> is of ''plait'': see ''plait'', ''plight''<sup>3</sup>.] To open; unfold.

{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 50.}}}}

¶
'''unplitable†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''unplite'' + ''-able''.] Intricate; complicated.
{{smaller block|Ther was establissed or cryed grevous and ''unplitable'' coempcion.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. prose 4.}}}}

'''unplucked''' (un-plukt′), ''a.'' Not plucked; not pulled or torn away. ''Fletcher (and another)'', Two Noble Kinsmen, v. 1.

'''unplug''' (un-plug′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''plug''.] To remove a plug from. See ''unplugged''.
{{smaller block|First, the resistance is measured in the usual manner with the other end of the cable earthed and with no plug in A, and balance is obtained by ''unplugging'' a resistance, R.
{{right|''Elect. Rev.'' (Eng.), XXV. 550.}}}}

'''unplugged''' (un-plugd′), ''a.'' Having the plug removed; also, not plugged: in electrical testing, said of a resistance when the plug which short-circuits the coils of wire forming the resistance in the box of resistance-coils is taken out.

'''unplumb<sup>1</sup>''' (un-plum′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''plumb''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.''] Not plumb; not vertical. ''Clarke.''

'''unplumb<sup>2</sup>''' (un-plum′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''plumb''<sup>2</sup>.] To deprive of lead; remove the lead from. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Their turpitude purveys to their malice; and they ''unplumb'' the dead for bullets to assassinate the living.
{{right|''Burke'', To a Noble Lord.}}}}

'''unplumbed''' (un-plumd′), ''a.'' Not plumbed or measured by a plumb-line; unfathomed.
{{smaller block|The ''unplumb’d'', salt, estranging sea.}}
readings.c2s2:
{{smaller block|{{right|''M. Arnold'', Switzerland, To Marguerite.}}}}

'''unplume''' (un-plöm′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''plume''.] To strip of plumes or feathers; degrade. ''Glanville.''

'''un poco''' (ön pō′kō). In ''music'', a little; slightly; somewhat: as, ''un poco staccato'', somewhat staccato; ''un poco ritardando'', retarding a little.

'''unpoetic''' (un-pọ̄-et′ik), ''a.'' Not poetic; unpoetical.

'''unpoetical''' (un-pọ̄-et′i-kal), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not poetical; not having or possessing poetical character; prosaic. ''T. Warton'', Hist. Eng. Poetry, III. 444. —'''2.''' Not proper to or becoming a poet. ''Bp. Corbet'', On the Death of Queen Anne.

'''unpoetically''' (un-pọ̄-et′i-kal-i), ''adv.'' In an unpoetical manner; prosaically.

'''unpoeticalness''' (un-pọ̄-et′i-kal-ne̤s), ''n.'' The character of being unpoetical.

'''unpointed''' (un-poin′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not having a point; not sharp.—'''2†.''' Having the points unfastened, as a doublet.
{{smaller block|His doublet loose and ''unpoynted.''
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 255.}}}}
'''3.''' Having no point or sting; wanting point or definite aim or purpose.
{{smaller block|The conclusion . . . here would have shown dull, flat, and ''unpointed.'' {{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetic Lady, iv. 3.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
'''4.''' Not having marks by which to distinguish sentences, members, and clauses; unpunctuated: as, ''unpointed'' writing.—'''5.''' Not having the vowel points or marks: as, an ''unpointed'' manuscript in Hebrew or Arabic.

{{smaller block|The reader of ''unpointed'' Hebrew . . . supplies for himself the vowels, by means of which alone the consonants can be raised into expressive sound.
{{right|''E. Caird'', Philos. of Kant, p. 203.}}}}

'''unpoised''' (un-poizd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not poised; not balanced.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oft on the brink
Of ruin . . .
Totter’d the rash democracy; ''unpois’d'',
And by the rage devour’d.</poem>
{{right|''Thomson'', Liberty.}}}}
'''2†.''' Unweighed; unhesitating; regardless of consequences.
{{smaller block|<poem>Seize on revenge, grasp the stern-bended front
Of frowning vengeance with ''unpaiz’d'' clutch.</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, II., iii. 1.}}}}

'''unpoison''' (un-poi′zn), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''poison.''] To remove or expel poison from; free from poison. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Such a course could not but in a short time have ''unpoisoned'' their perverted minds.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, V. i.}}}}

'''unpolicied''' (un-pol′i-sid), ''a.'' '''1.''' Destitute of civil polity or a regular form of government. ''Warburton'', Divine Legation, i. § 5.—'''2.''' Void of policy; impolitic; imprudent; stupid.

{{smaller block|<poem>That I might hear thee call great Cæsar ass
''Unpolicied!''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 2. 311.}}}}

'''unpolish''' (un-pol′ish), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''polish.''] '''1.''' To remove polish or gloss from, as varnished wood or blackened boots. ''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 9.—'''2.''' To deprive of politeness or elegance; render rough or inelegant.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unpleadable|6635|unpossibility}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''unpleadable''' (un-plē′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Unfit to be pleaded or urged as a plea. ''South'', Sermons, IX. vi.

'''unpleaded''' (un-plē′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not pleaded; not urged.—'''2.''' Undefended by an advocate. ''Otway.''

'''unpleasable''' (un-plē′za̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being pleased. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|My ''unpleasable'' daughter. {{right|''Burgoyne'', The Heiress, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unpleasance''' (un-plez′a̤ns), ''n.'' Lack of pleasance; displeasure.

'''unpleasant''' (un-plez′a̤nt), ''a.'' Not pleasant; not affording pleasure; disagreeable.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''unpleasant’st'' words
That ever blotted paper.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 2. 254.}}
We have also here and there remarked a little of that ''unpleasant'' trick . . . of telling a story by implication and allusion. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.}}
Men of worldly minds, finding the true way of life ''unpleasant'' to walk in, have attempted to find out other and easier roads. {{right|''J. H. Newman'', Parochial Sermons, i. 99.}}}}

'''unpleasantly''' (un-plez′a̤nt-li), ''adv.'' In an unpleasant manner; in a manner not pleasing; disagreeably.

'''unpleasantness''' (un-plez′a̤nt-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state or quality of being unpleasant; disagreeableness. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity.—'''2.''' A slight disagreement or falling out; a petty quarrel; an unimportant misunderstanding. [Colloq.] {{smaller|—'''The late unpleasantness,''' the civil war. [Humorous, U. S.]}}

{{smaller block|The weather-boarding in many places is riddled with bullets — cards left by passing visitors during ''the late unpleasantness.''{{right|''The Century'', XLI. 326.}}}}

'''unpleasantry''' (un-plez′a̤n-tri), ''n.'' '''1.''' Want of pleasantry; absence or the opposite of cheerfulness, humor, or gaiety; disagreeableness. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It would have been well for a man of so many peculiarities as Dr. Gower if this were all the ''unpleasantry'' to which he subjected himself.{{right|''Jon Bee'', Essay on Samuel Foote, p. xli.}}}}
'''2.''' An unpleasant occurrence; especially, a slight quarrel or falling out. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Now, on the other hand, the goddess and her establishment of hoaxers, at Eleusis, did a vast “stroke of business” for more than six centuries, without any ''unpleasantries'' occurring.{{right|''De Quincey'', Secret Societies, I.}}}}
{{smaller block|If . . . there are two such imperious and domineering spirits in a family, ''unpleasantries'' of course will arise from their contentions.{{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, I. xxxiii.}}}}
'''3.''' A discomfort. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The minor ''unpleasantries'' attending a hasty toilet.{{right|''Chambers’s Journal'', Oct. 9, 1858, p. 235. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''unpleased''' (un-plēzd′), ''a.'' Not pleased; displeased.
{{smaller block|My ''unpleased'' eye.{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 3. 193.}}}}

'''unpleasing''' (un-plē′zing), ''a.'' Unpleasant; offensive; disgusting; disagreeable; distasteful.

<poem>Despiteful tidings! O ''unpleasing'' news!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 1. 37.}}
A patch of sand is ''unpleasing''; a desert has all the awe of ocean. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 318.}}}}

'''unpleasingly''' (un-plē′zing-li), ''adv.'' In an unpleasing manner. ''Bp. Hall'', Death of Absalom.

'''unpleasingness''' (un-plē′zing-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unpleasing. ''Milton'', Divorce, ii. 21.

'''unpleasive†''' (un-plē′ziv), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''pleasive'', < ''please'' + ''-ive''.] Not pleasing; unpleasant.
{{smaller block|Grief is never but an ''unpleasive'' passion.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Remains, p. 108.}}}}

'''unpleasurable''' (un-plezh′ṳ̄r-a-bl), ''a.'' Not pleasurable; not giving pleasure. ''Coleridge.''

'''unpleasurably''' (un-plezh′ṳ̄r-a-bli), ''adv.'' So as not to give pleasure; without pleasure.
{{smaller block|So, as Lady Jackson rewrites the old story once more, one reads it, if but for its subject, not altogether unprofitably or ''unpleasurably''. {{right|''The Academy'', May, 1890.}}}}

'''unpliable''' (un-plī′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not pliable. ''Holland.''

'''unpliably''' (un-plī′a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unpliable manner; without yielding.

'''unpliant''' (un-plī′ant), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not pliant; not easily bent; stiff.
{{smaller block|The ''unpliant'' bow. {{right|''Cowper'', Odyssey, xxi.}}}}
'''2.''' Not readily yielding the will; not compliant.
{{smaller block|A stubborn, ''unpliant'' morality. {{right|''Tatler'', No. 114.}}}}

'''unpliantly''' (un-plī′ant-li), ''adv.'' In an unpliant manner; uncompliäntly.

'''unplight<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''unpliȝt''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> (intensive) + ''plight''<sup>1</sup>.] Peril.

{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 50.}}}}

{{smaller block|First, the resistance is measured in the usual manner with the other end of the cable earthed and with no plug in A, and balance is obtained by ''unplugging'' a resistance, R.
{{right|''Elect. Rev.'' (Eng.), XXV. 550.}}}}

'''unplumb<sup>1</sup>''' (un-plum′), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''plumb''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.''] Not plumb; not vertical. ''Clarke.''

'''unplumb<sup>2</sup>''' (un-plum′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''plumb''<sup>2</sup>.] To deprive of lead; remove the lead from. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Their turpitude purveys to their malice; and they ''unplumb'' the dead for bullets to assassinate the living.
{{right|''Burke'', To a Noble Lord.}}}}

'''unplumbed''' (un-plumd′), ''a.'' Not plumbed or measured by a plumb-line; unfathomed.
{{smaller block|The ''unplumb’d'', salt, estranging sea. {{right|''M. Arnold'', Switzerland, To Marguerite.}}}}

'''unplume''' (un-plöm′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''plume''.] To strip of plumes or feathers; degrade. ''Glanville.''

'''un poco''' (ön pō′kō). In ''music'', a little; slightly; somewhat: as, ''un poco staccato'', somewhat staccato; ''un poco ritardando'', retarding a little.

'''unpoetic''' (un-pọ̄-et′ik), ''a.'' Not poetic; unpoetical.

'''unpoetical''' (un-pọ̄-et′i-kal), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not poetical; not having or possessing poetical character; prosaic. ''T. Warton'', Hist. Eng. Poetry, III. 444. —'''2.''' Not proper to or becoming a poet. ''Bp. Corbet'', On the Death of Queen Anne.

'''unpoetically''' (un-pọ̄-et′i-kal-i), ''adv.'' In an unpoetical manner; prosaically.

'''unpoeticalness''' (un-pọ̄-et′i-kal-ne̤s), ''n.'' The character of being unpoetical.

'''unpointed''' (un-poin′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not having a point; not sharp.—'''2†.''' Having the points unfastened, as a doublet.
{{smaller block|His doublet loose and ''unpoynted.''
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 255.}}}}
'''3.''' Having no point or sting; wanting point or definite aim or purpose.
{{smaller block|The conclusion . . . here would have shown dull, flat, and ''unpointed.'' {{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetic Lady, iv. 3.}}}} '''4.''' Not having marks by which to distinguish sentences, members, and clauses; unpunctuated: as, ''unpointed'' writing.—'''5.''' Not having the vowel points or marks: as, an ''unpointed'' manuscript in Hebrew or Arabic.

{{smaller block|The reader of ''unpointed'' Hebrew . . . supplies for himself the vowels, by means of which alone the consonants can be raised into expressive sound.
{{right|''E. Caird'', Philos. of Kant, p. 203.}}}}

'''unpoised''' (un-poizd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not poised; not balanced.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oft on the brink
Of ruin . . .
Totter’d the rash democracy; ''unpois’d'',
And by the rage devour’d.</poem>
{{right|''Thomson'', Liberty.}}}}
'''2†.''' Unweighed; unhesitating; regardless of consequences.
{{smaller block|<poem>Seize on revenge, grasp the stern-bended front
Of frowning vengeance with ''unpaiz’d'' clutch.</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, II., iii. 1.}}}}

'''unpoison''' (un-poi′zn), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''poison.''] To remove or expel poison from; free from poison. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Such a course could not but in a short time have ''unpoisoned'' their perverted minds.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, V. i.}}}}

'''unpolicied''' (un-pol′i-sid), ''a.'' '''1.''' Destitute of civil polity or a regular form of government. ''Warburton'', Divine Legation, i. § 5.—'''2.''' Void of policy; impolitic; imprudent; stupid.

<poem>That I might hear thee call great Cæsar ass
''Unpolicied!''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 2. 311.}}}}

'''unpolish''' (un-pol′ish), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''polish.''] '''1.''' To remove polish or gloss from, as varnished wood or blackened boots. ''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 9.—'''2.''' To deprive of politeness or elegance; render rough or inelegant.

{{smaller block|How anger ''unpolishes'' the most polite!
{{right|''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, V. 286. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unpolished''' (un-pol′isht), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not polished; not brought to a polish: noting surfaces of marble, wood, metal, etc.
{{smaller block|''Unpolish’d'' gems no ray on pride bestow.
{{right|''Pope'', On his Grotto.}}}}
'''2.''' Deprived of polish.—'''3.''' Not refined in manners; uncivilized; rude; plain.
{{smaller block|Those first ''unpolish’d'' matrons, big and bold.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, vi. 12.}}}}

'''unpolite''' (un-pọ̄-līt′), ''a.'' Not polite; not refined in manners; uncivil; rude; impolite. ''Tatler'', No. 140.

'''unpolitely''' (un-pọ̄-līt′li), ''adv.'' Impolitely.
{{smaller block|Rather conscious and confused, Arthur asked his pardon if he had stared at him ''unpolitely''.
{{right|''Dickens'', Little Dorrit, xxiii.}}}}

'''unpoliteness''' (un-pọ̄-līt′nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' Lack of polish; want of refinement; coarseness, as of a style of writing.
{{smaller block|Sad outcries are made of the ''unpoliteness'' of the style.
{{right|''Blackwall'', Sacred Classics Defended.}}}}
'''2.''' Impoliteness.

'''unpolitic''' (un-pol′i-tik), ''a.'' Impolitic.

'''unpolled''' (un-pōld′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not polled; not registered or counted: as, a large ''unpolled'' vote.
{{smaller block|The opposite party bribed the bar-maid at the Town Arms to hocus the brandy and water of fourteen ''unpolled'' electors. {{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
'''2†.''' Unplundered; not stripped.
{{smaller block|Richer than ''unpoll’d'' Arabian wealth and Indian gold.
{{right|''Fanshawe'', Poems (1673), p. 314.}}}}

'''unpolluted''' (un-pọ-lū′ted), ''a.'' Not polluted; not defiled; not corrupted; pure; unspotted.
{{smaller block|Her fair and ''unpolluted'' flesh. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 1. 262.}}}}

'''unpope''' (un-pōp′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''pope''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To divest or deprive of the office, authority, and dignities of pope. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>So, guilty! So, remains I punish guilt!
He is ''unpoped'', and all he did I damn.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 170.}}}}
'''2.''' To deprive of a pope. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Rome will never so far ''unpope'' herself as to part with her pretended supremacy. {{right|''Fuller.''}}}}

'''unpopular''' (un-pop′ụ̄-lạ̈r), ''a.'' Not popular; not having the public favor: as, an ''unpopular'' magistrate; an ''unpopular'' law.
{{smaller block|We never could very clearly understand how it is that egotism, so ''unpopular'' in conversation, should be so popular in writing. {{right|''Macaulay'', Moore’s Byron.}}}}

'''unpopularity''' (un-pop-ụ̄-lar′ị-ti), ''n.'' The state of being unpopular. ''Burke'', Speech on Econ. Reform.

'''unpopularly''' (un-pop′ụ̄-lạ̈r-li), ''adv.'' In an unpopular manner; not popularly.

'''unportable†''' (un-pōr′tạ-bl), ''a.'' [ME. ''unportable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''portable''.] '''1.''' Not portable or capable of being carried. ''Raleigh.''—'''2.''' Not bearable, as a trouble; insupportable.
{{smaller block|Wherfore the seyd William, nothyr hese frendes . . . durst not, ne yet ne dar not rydyn ne goo abowte swyche occupacion as he arn used and disposed, to here [their] grete and ''unportable'' drede and vexacion. {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 17.}}}}

'''unportioned''' (un-pōr′shọnd), ''a.'' Not endowed or furnished with a portion or fortune.
{{smaller block|<poem>Has virtue charms? I grant her heavenly fair,
But if ''unportioned'', all will interest wed.</poem>
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, vii.}}}}

'''unportuous''' (un-pōr′ṳ̄-us), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''portuous'', < L. ''portuosus'', full of ports, < ''portus'', port: see ''port''<sup>1</sup>.] Having no ports. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|An ''unportuous'' coast. {{right|''Burke'', A Regicide Peace, iii.}}}}

'''unpositive''' (un-poz′i-tiv), ''a.'' Not positive; not assertive.
{{smaller block|A dumb, ''unpositive'' life, under the power of the world.
{{right|''H. Bushnell'', Sermons for the New Life, xvii.}}}}

'''unpossessed''' (un-pọ-zest′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not possessed; not owned; not held; not occupied.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such vast room in nature ''unpossessed''
By living soul.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., viii. 153.}}}}
'''2.''' Not in possession: used with ''of.''
{{smaller block|The mind, ''unpossessed of'' virtue.
{{right|''V. Knox'', Christian Philosophy, § 23.}}
The head is entirely ''unpossessed of'' ciliated lobes.
{{right|''W. B. Carpenter'', Micros., p. 453.}}}}

'''unpossessing†''' (un-pọ-zes′ing), ''a.'' Having no possessions.
{{smaller block|Thou ''unpossessing'' bastard! {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, ii. 1. 69.}}}}

'''unpossibility''' (un-pos-i-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' Impossibility. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It would be a matter of utter ''unpossibility''.
{{right|''Poe'', King Pest.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
